questions.questionText: Suppose $X$ is a random variable with finite variance. For $0<\theta<1$ and $n>3$, let $X_{1}=X$, $X_{2}=\theta X_{1}, X_{3}=\theta X_{2}, \ldots, X_{n}=\theta X_{n-1}$. Then $\operatorname{Corr}\left(X_{1}, X_{n}\right)$ is $1$ $-1$ $\theta^{n-2}$ $\theta^{n-3}$
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose $X$ is a random variable with finite variance. For $0<\theta<1$ and $n>3$, let $X_{1}=X$, $X_{2}=\theta X_{1}, X_{3}=\theta X_{2}, \ldots, X_{n}=\theta X_{n-1}$. Then $\operatorname{Corr}\left(X_{1}, X_{n}\right)$ is

  1. $1$
     
  2. $-1$
     
  3. $\theta^{n-2}$
     
  4. $\theta^{n-3}$
questions.explanation: Explanation: We are given that $$ X_{k}=\theta^{k-1} X \quad \text { for } k=1,2, \ldots, n $$ So, $$ X_{1}=X, \quad X_{n}=\theta^{n-1} X $$ Covariance $$ \operatorname{Cov}\left(X_{1}, X_{n}\right)=\operatorname{Cov}\left(X, \theta^{n-1} X\right)=\theta^{n-1} \operatorname{Var}(X) $$ Variances $$ \operatorname{Var}\left(X_{1}\right)=\operatorname{Var}(X), \quad \operatorname{Var}\left(X_{n}\right)=\theta^{2(n-1)} \operatorname{Var}(X) $$ Correlation $$$$ \begin{equation*} \operatorname{Corr}\left(X_{1}, X_{n}\right)=\frac{\theta^{n-1} \operatorname{Var}(X)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X) \cdot \theta^{2(n-1)} \operatorname{Var}(X)}}=\frac{\theta^{n-1}}{\theta^{n-1}}= 1 \end{equation*} $$$$ GO Classes answered Jun 27, 2025 • edited Jun 27, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionHtml:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with probability density function
                                                               

                                                                              $f(x)=\frac{1}{2} e^{-|x-1|}, \quad-\infty<x<\infty$

Then the value of $P(1<|X|<2)$ is:
 

  1. $\left(e^{-1}-e^{-2}\right)^{2}$
     
  2. $ \frac{1}{2}\left(e^{-1}+e\right)\left(e^{-1}-e^{-2}\right)$
     
  3. $\left(e^{-1}+e\right)\left(e^{-1}-e^{-2}\right)$
     
  4. $\frac{1}{2}\left(e^{-2}+e^{-1}\right)$
questions.explanation: $$ \begin{aligned} P(1<|X|<2) & =P(-2<X<-1)+P(1<X<2) \\ & =\int_{-2}^{-1} \frac{1}{2} e^{-|x-1|} \mathrm{d} x+\int_{1}^{2} \frac{1}{2} e^{-|x-1|} \mathrm{d} x \\ & =\underbrace{\int_{-2}^{-1} \frac{1}{2} e^{x-1} \mathrm{~d} x}_{\text {since } x<1 \Rightarrow|x-1|=1-x}+\underbrace{\int_{1}^{2} \frac{1}{2} e^{-(x-1)} \mathrm{d} x}_{\text {since } x>1 \Rightarrow|x-1|=x-1} \\ & =\int_{-2}^{-1} \frac{1}{2} e^{x-1} \mathrm{~d} x+\int_{1}^{2} \frac{1}{2} e^{1-x} \mathrm{~d} x \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \int_{-2}^{-1} e^{x-1} \mathrm{~d} x+\frac{1}{2} \int_{1}^{2} e^{1-x} \mathrm{~d} x \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\left[e^{-1}\left(e^{-1}-e^{-2}\right)+e\left(e^{-1}-e^{-2}\right)\right] \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\left(e^{-1}+e\right)\left(e^{-1}-e^{-2}\right) \end{aligned} $$ GO Classes answered Jun 27, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow See 1 comment 1 1 comment reply Inder_129 commented Dec 11, 2025 reply Follow flag wrong answer 0 0 reply Share Please log in or reg

questions.excerpt: Let the random variable $X \sim B(5, p)$ such that $P(X=2)=2 P(X=3)$. Then the variance of $X$ is$\frac{10}{3}$ $\frac{10}{9}$ $\frac{5}{3}$ $\frac{5}{9}$
questions.questionText: Let the random variable $X \sim B(5, p)$ such that $P(X=2)=2 P(X=3)$. Then the variance of $X$ is $\frac{10}{3}$ $\frac{10}{9}$ $\frac{5}{3}$ $\frac{5}{9}$
questions.questionHtml:
Let the random variable $X \sim B(5, p)$ such that $P(X=2)=2 P(X=3)$. Then the variance of $X$ is

  1. $\frac{10}{3}$
     
  2. $\frac{10}{9}$
     
  3. $\frac{5}{3}$
     
  4. $\frac{5}{9}$
questions.explanation: We are given that $X \sim \operatorname{Bin}(5, p)$. The binomial probability mass function is: $$ P(X=k)=\binom{5}{k} p^{k}(1-p)^{5-k} $$ Using the condition $P(X=2)=2 P(X=3)$, we write: $$ \binom{5}{2} p^{2}(1-p)^{3}=2 \cdot\binom{5}{3} p^{3}(1-p)^{2} $$ Substituting binomial coefficients: $$ \begin{gathered} 10 \cdot p^{2}(1-p)^{3}=2 \cdot 10 \cdot p^{3}(1-p)^{2} \\ p^{2}(1-p)^{3}=2 p^{3}(1-p)^{2} \end{gathered} $$ Canceling common factors $\left(p^{2}\right.$ and $\left.(1-p)^{2}\right)$ : $$ (1-p)=2 p \Rightarrow 1-p=2 p \Rightarrow 1=3 p \Rightarrow p=\frac{1}{3} $$ Now, compute the variance of $X \sim B(n, p)$, which is: $$ \operatorname{Var}(X)=n p(1-p)=5 \cdot \frac{1}{3} \cdot\left(1-\frac{1}{3}\right)=5 \cdot \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{2}{3}=\frac{10}{9} $$ GO Classes answered Jun 27, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent $\operatorname{Bin}\left(3, \frac{1}{3}\right)$ random variables. Then the probability that the matrix $$ P=\left(\begin{array}{cc} \frac{X}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{Y}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{array}\right) $$ is orthogonal, is $\frac{5}{9}$ $\frac{65}{81}$ $\frac{4}{9}$ $\frac{16}{81}$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent $\operatorname{Bin}\left(3, \frac{1}{3}\right)$ random variables. Then the probability that the matrix
$$
P=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\frac{X}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{Y}{\sqrt{2}} \\
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\end{array}\right)
$$
is orthogonal, is

  1. $\frac{5}{9}$
     
  2. $\frac{65}{81}$
     
  3. $\frac{4}{9}$
     
  4. $\frac{16}{81}$
questions.explanation: $$ P=\left(\begin{array}{cc} \frac{X}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{Y}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{array}\right) $$ For $P$ to be orthogonal, its columns must be orthonormal. Let $$ \mathbf{c}_{1}=\left[\begin{array}{c} \frac{X}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{array}\right], \quad \mathbf{c}_{2}=\left[\begin{array}{c} \frac{Y}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{array}\right] . $$ Then their inner product must be zero: $$ \mathbf{c}_{1}^{\top} \mathbf{c}_{2}=\frac{X Y}{2}-\frac{1}{2} . $$ Matrix is orthogonal $\Longleftrightarrow$ inner product of columns is 0 : $$ \begin{gathered} \frac{X Y}{2}-\frac{1}{2}=0 \Rightarrow X Y=1 \\ \mathbb{P}(X Y=1)=\mathbb{P}(X=1) \cdot \mathbb{P}(Y=1) \\ \mathbb{P}(X=1)=\binom{3}{1}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{2}=3 \cdot \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{4}{9}=\frac{4}{9} \\ \mathbb{P}(X Y=1)=\left(\frac{4} {9}\right)^{2}=\frac{16}{81} \\ \end{gathered} $$ GO Classes answered Jun 27, 2025 GO Classes comment

questions.questionText: Let $U_{1}, U_{2}, \ldots, U_{n}$ be independent and identically distributed random variables with $U_{i} \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)$. Define the random variable $Z=\max \left(U_{1}, U_{2}, \ldots, U_{n}\right)$. The cumulative distribution function (CDF) of $Z$ is given by: $$ F_{Z}(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cl} 0 & x<0 \\ ? & 0 \leq x \leq 1 \\ 1 & x>1 \end{array}\right. $$ What is the correct expression to fill in the missing part of the CDF (i.e., for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ )? $x^{n}$ $1-x^{n}$ $n x^{n-1}$ $1-(1-x)^{n}$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $U_{1}, U_{2}, \ldots, U_{n}$ be independent and identically distributed random variables with $U_{i} \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)$.
Define the random variable $Z=\max \left(U_{1}, U_{2}, \ldots, U_{n}\right)$.
The cumulative distribution function (CDF) of $Z$ is given by:
$$
F_{Z}(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cl}
0 & x<0 \\
? & 0 \leq x \leq 1 \\
1 & x>1
\end{array}\right.
$$
What is the correct expression to fill in the missing part of the CDF (i.e., for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ )?

  1. $x^{n}$
     
  2. $1-x^{n}$
     
  3. $n x^{n-1}$
     
  4. $1-(1-x)^{n}$
questions.explanation: Explanation: $$ \begin{aligned} F_{Z}(x) & =\mathbb{P}(Z \leq x) \\ & =\mathbb{P}\left(\max \left(U_{1}, U_{2}, \ldots, U_{n}\right) \leq x\right) \\ & =\mathbb{P}\left(U_{1} \leq x, U_{2} \leq x, \ldots, U_{n} \leq x\right) \end{aligned} $$ Each $\mathbb{P}\left(U_{i} \leq x\right)=x$, so by independence: $$ F_{Z}(x)=x^{n} $$ GO Classes answered Jun 27, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable. $X$ has a constant PDF on $(0,1]$, and another constant PDF on $(1,2]$. The PDF of $X$ is given by:                                                                                    $f_X(x)= \begin{cases}c & \text { for } 0<x \leq 1 \\ d & \text { for } 1<x \leq 2 \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}$ It is known that                                                                                $\mathbb{P}(1 \leq X \leq 2)=2 \cdot \mathbb{P}(0 \leq X<1) $ What are the values of $c$ and $d$ ? $\quad c=1 / 2, \quad d=1 / 2$ $\quad c=1 / 3, \quad d=2 / 3$ $\quad c=2 / 3, \quad d=1 / 3$ $\quad c=1 / 4, \quad d=3 / 4$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable.
$X$ has a constant PDF on $(0,1]$, and another constant PDF on $(1,2]$.
The PDF of $X$ is given by:
                                                                                   $f_X(x)= \begin{cases}c & \text { for } 0<x \leq 1 \\ d & \text { for } 1<x \leq 2 \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}$
It is known that

                                                                               $\mathbb{P}(1 \leq X \leq 2)=2 \cdot \mathbb{P}(0 \leq X<1)

$

What are the values of $c$ and $d$ ?
 

  1. $\quad c=1 / 2, \quad d=1 / 2$
  2. $\quad c=1 / 3, \quad d=2 / 3$
  3. $\quad c=2 / 3, \quad d=1 / 3$
  4. $\quad c=1 / 4, \quad d=3 / 4$
questions.explanation: Since the PDF is constant over each interval, the probability over each interval is just the height times the width: $\mathbb{P}(0<X \leq 1)=c \cdot 1=c$ $\mathbb{P}(1<X \leq 2)=d \cdot 1=d$ From the condition, $d=2 c$. Also, the total probability must be 1 , so: $$ c+d=1 $$ Substituting $d=2 c$ gives: $$ c+2 c=1 \Rightarrow 3 c=1 \Rightarrow c=\frac{1}{3}, \quad d=\frac{2}{3} $$ GO Classes answered Jun 27, 2025 • edited Jul 16, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. What is the p.d.f. of $Y$ ? $g(y)=3 y^{2}, \quad 0 \leq y \leq 1$ $g(y)=6 y^{5}, \quad 0 \leq y \leq 1$ $g(y)=6 y^{4}, \quad 0 \leq y \leq 1$ $g(y)=9 y^{4}, \quad 0 \leq y \leq 1$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with probability density function:
$$
f_{X}(x)=3 x^{2} \quad \text { for } 0 \leq x \leq 1 .
$$
Define a new random variable $Y=\sqrt{X}$.
What is the p.d.f. of $Y$ ?

  1. $g(y)=3 y^{2}, \quad 0 \leq y \leq 1$
     
  2. $g(y)=6 y^{5}, \quad 0 \leq y \leq 1$
     
  3. $g(y)=6 y^{4}, \quad 0 \leq y \leq 1$
     
  4. $g(y)=9 y^{4}, \quad 0 \leq y \leq 1$
questions.explanation: To begin, we find the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of $Y$. The probability that $Y \leq y$ is the same as the probability that $\sqrt{X} \leq y$, which is the same as $X \leq y^{2}$. So: $$ G(y)=\operatorname{Pr}(Y \leq y)=\operatorname{Pr}\left(X \leq y^{2}\right)=\int_{0}^{y^{2}} 3 x^{2} d x $$ Evaluating the integral: $$ G(y)=3 \cdot\left[\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{y^{2}}=y^{6} $$ Now to find the pdf $g(y)$, we differentiate the CDF: $$ g(y)=\frac{d}{d y} G(y)=\frac{d}{d y}\left(y^{6}\right)=6 y^{5} $$ So the pdf of $Y=\sqrt{X}$ is: $$ g(y)=6 y^{5} \quad \text { for } 0 \leq y \leq 1 $$ GO Classes answered Jun 27, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Let $U$ be a continuous random variable uniformly distributed over the interval $[-1,2]$. What is the value of the expected value $E[U(U-1)]$ ?

  2. $\frac{1}{2}$
     
  3. $0$
     
  4. $\frac{2}{3}$
questions.explanation: Given: $U \sim$ Uniform $(-1,2)$, so the probability density function is: $$ f_{U}(u)=\frac{1}{2-(-1)}=\frac{1}{3}, \quad \text { for } u \in[-1,2] $$ We are asked to compute $E[U(U-1)]$. $$ E[U(U-1)]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(u) f_{U}(u) d u=\int_{-1}^{2} u(u-1) \cdot \frac{1}{3} d u $$ Now simplify the integrand: $$ \begin{gathered} u(u-1)=u^{2}-u \\ E[U(U-1)]=\frac{1}{3} \int_{-1}^{2}\left(u^{2}-u\right) d u=\frac{1}{3}\left[\frac{u^{3}}{3}-\frac{u^{2}}{2}\right]_{-1}^{2} \\ =\frac{1}{3}\left(\left(\frac{8}{3}-2\right)-\left(-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\right)\right)=\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{5}{6}\right)=\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{9}{6}=\frac{1}{2} \end{gathered} $$ GO Classes answered Jun 27, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables taking values in $\{1,2\}$, with joint distribution given by: $$ \begin{array}{ll} \operatorname{Pr}[X=1, Y=1]=\frac{1}{2}, & \operatorname{Pr}[X=1, Y=2]=\frac{1}{10} \\ \operatorname{Pr}[X=2, Y=1]=\frac{1}{10}, & \operatorname{Pr}[X=2, Y=2]=\frac{3}{10} \end{array} $$ What is the value of $\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y=1]$ ? $3 / 2$ $6 / 5$ $7 / 6$ $5 / 4$
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables taking values in $\{1,2\}$, with joint distribution given by:
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\operatorname{Pr}[X=1, Y=1]=\frac{1}{2}, & \operatorname{Pr}[X=1, Y=2]=\frac{1}{10} \\
\operatorname{Pr}[X=2, Y=1]=\frac{1}{10}, & \operatorname{Pr}[X=2, Y=2]=\frac{3}{10}
\end{array}
$$
What is the value of $\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y=1]$ ?

  1. $3 / 2$
  2. $6 / 5$
  3. $7 / 6$
  4. $5 / 4$
questions.explanation: Explanation: $$ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{Pr}[Y=1]=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{10}=\frac{6}{10} \\ \operatorname{Pr}[X=1 \mid Y=1]=\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{6}{10}}=\frac{5}{6}, \quad \operatorname{Pr}[X=2 \mid Y=1]=\frac{\frac{1}{10}}{\frac{6}{10}}=\frac{1}{6} \\ \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y=1]=1 \cdot \frac{5}{6}+2 \cdot \frac{1}{6}=\frac{5}{6}+\frac{2}{6}=\frac{7}{6} \end{gathered} $$ GO Classes answered Jun 27, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Let $X$ be Poisson(2) and $Y$ be Binomial(10,3/4) random variables. If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $P(X Y=0)$ is $e^{-2}+\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{10}\left(1-e^{-2}\right)$ $e^{-2}+\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{10}\left(1-2 e^{-2}\right)$ $e^{-2}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{10}$ $e^{-2}+1-\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{10}$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $X$ be Poisson(2) and $Y$ be Binomial(10,3/4) random variables. If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $P(X Y=0)$ is

  1. $e^{-2}+\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{10}\left(1-e^{-2}\right)$
     
  2. $e^{-2}+\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{10}\left(1-2 e^{-2}\right)$
     
  3. $e^{-2}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{10}$
     
  4. $e^{-2}+1-\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{10}$
questions.explanation: The required probability is given by $$ \begin{aligned} P(X Y=0)= & \sum_{y=0}^{10} P(X=0, Y=y)+\sum_{x=1}^{\infty} P(X=x, Y=0) \\ = & \sum_{y=0}^{10} P(X=0) P(Y=y)+\sum_{x=1}^{\infty} P(X=x) P(Y=0) \\ & \quad(\text { using independence of } X \text { and } Y) \\ = & P(X=0) \sum_{y=0}^{10} P(Y=y)+P(Y=0)(1-P(X=0)) \\ = & e^{-2} \times 1+\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{10}\left(1-e^{-2}\right) \\ = & e^{-2}+\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{10}\left(1-e^{-2}\right) \end{aligned} $$ Hence option (A) is the correct choice. Optional Solution: The required probability is given by $$ \begin{aligned} P(X Y=0)= & P(X=0 \text { or } Y=0) \\ = & P(X=0)+P(Y=0)-P(X=0, Y=0) \\ = & P(X=0)+P(Y=0)-P(X=0) P(Y=0) \\ & \quad \quad \text { (using independence of } X \text { and } Y) \\ = & P(X=0)+P(Y=0)(1-P(X=0)) \\ = & e^{-2}+\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{10}\left(1-e^{-2}\right) \end{aligned} $$ Hence option (A) is the correct choice.

questions.questionHtml:
Let $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ be i.i.d. Poisson random variables with mean 1. Then $P\left(\max \left(X_{1}, X_{2}\right)>1\right)=$

  1. $1-e^{-2}$
     
  2. $1-2 e^{-2}$
     
  3. $1-3 e^{-2}$
     
  4. $1-4 e^{-2}$
questions.explanation: We use the identity: $$ P\left(\max \left(X_{1}, X_{2}\right)>1\right)=1-P\left(\max \left(X_{1}, X_{2}\right) \leq 1\right)=1-P\left(X_{1} \leq 1, X_{2} \leq 1\right) $$ Since $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ are independent, $$ P\left(X_{1} \leq 1, X_{2} \leq 1\right)=P\left(X_{1} \leq 1\right) \cdot P\left(X_{2} \leq 1\right)=[P(X \leq 1)]^{2} $$ Now for $X \sim$ Poisson(1), we have $$ P(X \leq 1)=P(X=0)+P(X=1)=e^{-1} \cdot\left(\frac{1^{0}}{0!}+\frac{1^{1}}{1!}\right)=e^{-1}(1+1)=2 e^{-1} $$ Therefore, $$ P\left(X_{1} \leq 1, X_{2} \leq 1\right)=\left(2 e^{-1}\right)^{2}=4 e^{-2} $$ Finally, $$ P\left(\max \left(X_{1}, X_{2}\right)>1\right)=1-4 e^{-2} $$ GO Classes answered Jun 27, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow See 1 comment 1 1 comment reply Akashsr3 commented 5 days ago reply Follow flag Why did we take P(x1) whole squared ? and if we choosing one of them as maximum then shouldnt it be just P(x1) or P(x2) ? 0 0 reply Share Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionHtml:
Let $X$ and $Y$ denote the lifetimes (in years) of two independent components connected in a series with respective probability density functions
$$
f_{X}(x)=\frac{1}{2} e^{-\frac{x}{2}}, x>0 \quad \text { and } \quad f_{Y}(y)=\frac{y}{4} e^{-\frac{y}{2}}, y>0
$$
Then the probability that the system will survive for at least 2 years, is

  1. $e^{-2}$
     
  2. $2 e^{-2}$
     
  3. $3 e^{-2}$
     
  4. $4 e^{-2}$.
questions.explanation: The required probability is given by $$ \begin{aligned} P(\min (X, Y) \geq 2) & =P(X \geq 2, Y \geq 2) \\ & =P(X \geq 2) P(Y \geq 2) \quad \text { (since } X \text { and } Y \text { are independent) } \\ & =\left(\int_{2}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2} e^{-\frac{x}{2}} \mathrm{~d} x\right)\left(\int_{2}^{\infty} \frac{y}{4} e^{-\frac{y}{2}} \mathrm{~d} y\right) \\ & =\left[-e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\right]_{2}^{\infty} \frac{1}{4}\left(\left[-2 y e^{-\frac{y}{2}}\right]_{2}^{\infty}+\int_{2}^{\infty} 2 e^{-\frac{y}{2}} \mathrm{~d} y\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{4} e^{-1}\left(4 e^{-1}+2\left[-2 e^{-\frac{y}{2}}\right]_{2}^{\infty}\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{4} e^{-1}\left(4 e^{-1}+4 e^{-1}\right) \\ & =2 e^{-2} \end{aligned} $$ Hence option (B) is the correct choice.

questions.questionText: Let $Y$ be an exponential random variable with mean $1 / \theta$, where $\theta>0$. The conditional distribution of $X$ given $Y$ has Poisson distribution with mean $Y$. Then, the variance of $X$ is $\frac{1}{\theta^{2}}$ $\frac{\theta+1}{\theta}$ $\frac{\theta^{2}+1}{\theta^{2}}$ $\frac{\theta+1}{\theta^{2}}$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $Y$ be an exponential random variable with mean $1 / \theta$, where $\theta>0$. The conditional distribution of $X$ given $Y$ has Poisson distribution with mean $Y$. Then, the variance of $X$ is

  1. $\frac{1}{\theta^{2}}$
     
  2. $\frac{\theta+1}{\theta}$
     
  3. $\frac{\theta^{2}+1}{\theta^{2}}$
     
  4. $\frac{\theta+1}{\theta^{2}}$
questions.explanation: Since the conditional distribution of $X$ given $Y$ has Poisson distribution with mean $Y$, it follows that $E(X \mid Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Y)=Y$. Now, the variance of $X$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(X) & =E(\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Y))+\operatorname{Var}(E(X \mid Y)) \\ & =E(Y)+\operatorname{Var}(Y) \\ & =\frac{1}{\theta}+\frac{1}{\theta^{2}} \\ & =\frac{\theta+1}{\theta^{2}} \end{aligned} $$ Hence option (D) is the correct choice.

questions.questionText: Activities $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ form the critical path for a project with a PERT network. The means and variances of the activity duration for each activity are given below. All activity durations follow the Gaussian (normal) distribution, and are independent of each other. $Activity$ $A$ $B$ $C$ $D$ $Mean(days)$ $6$ $11$ $8$ $15$ $Variance $$\left(\right.$ days $\left.^2\right)$ $4$ $9$ $4$ $9$ The probability that the project will be completed within $40$ days is : (round off to two decimal places). (Note: Probability is a number between 0 and 1 ).
questions.questionHtml:
Activities $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ form the critical path for a project with a PERT network. The means and variances of the activity duration for each activity are given below. All activity durations follow the Gaussian (normal) distribution, and are independent of each other.

$Activity$$A$$B$$C$$D$
$Mean(days)$$6$$11$$8$$15$
$Variance $$\left(\right.$ days $\left.^2\right)$$4$$9$$4$$9$


The probability that the project will be completed within $40$ days is :

(round off to two decimal places).

(Note: Probability is a number between 0 and 1 ).
questions.explanation: Since the critical path consists of $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow D$ : Total mean duration: $$ \mu=6+11+8+15=40 \text { days } $$ Total variance: $$ \sigma^{2}=4+9+4+9=26 \text { days }^{2} $$ Let $T \sim \mathcal{N}(40,26)$, i.e., normal distribution with mean 40 and variance $=26$. We want: $$ P(T \leq 40) $$ Now, intuitively, for any normal distribution: The mean is the center of the bell curve. So, exactly half the probability lies to the left of the mean. Therefore, $$ P(T \leq 40)=0.5 $$ GO Classes answered Jun 27, 2025 • edited Jul 16, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: You have a fair five-sided die. The sides of the die are numbered from 1 to 5. Each die roll is independent of all others, and all faces are equally likely to come out on top when the die is rolled. Suppose you roll the die twice. Let event $A$ be "the total of two rolls is 10", event $B$ be "at least one roll resulted in 5", and event $C$ be "at least one roll resulted in $1^{\prime \prime}$. Which of the following statements are correct? Events $A$ and $B$ are independent. Events $A$ and $C$ are independent. Events $A$ and $B$ are not independent. Events $A$ and $C$ are not independent.
questions.questionHtml:
You have a fair five-sided die. The sides of the die are numbered from 1 to 5. Each die roll is independent of all others, and all faces are equally likely to come out on top when the die is rolled. Suppose you roll the die twice.

Let event $A$ be "the total of two rolls is 10", event $B$ be "at least one roll resulted in 5", and event $C$ be "at least one roll resulted in $1^{\prime \prime}$.

Which of the following statements are correct?

  1. Events $A$ and $B$ are independent.
  2. Events $A$ and $C$ are independent.
  3. Events $A$ and $B$ are not independent.
  4. Events $A$ and $C$ are not independent.
questions.explanation: Overall, there are 25 different outcomes in the sample space. For a total of 10 , we should get a 5 on both rolls. Therefore $A \subset B$, and $$ \mathbf{P}(B \mid A)=\frac{\mathbf{P}(A \cap B)}{\mathbf{P}(A)}=\frac{\mathbf{P}(A)}{\mathbf{P}(A)}=1 $$ We observe that to get at least one 5 showing, we can have 5 on the first roll, 5 on the second roll, or 5 on both rolls, which corresponds to 9 distinct outcomes in the sample space. Therefore $$ \mathbf{P}(B)=\frac{9}{25} \neq \mathbf{P}(B \mid A) $$ ii. No Given event $A$, we know that both roll outcomes must be 5. Therefore, we could not have event $C$ occur, which would require at least one 1 showing. Formally, there are 9 outcomes in $C$, and $$ \mathbf{P}(C)=\frac{9}{25} $$ But $$ \mathbf{P}(C \mid A)=0 \neq \mathbf{P}(C) $$ GO Classes answered Jun 23, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 1 1 vote option C and D Captain Price answered Jun 20, 2025 • edited Jun 22, 2025 by Ca

If he misses the forecast, Victor will flip a fair coin to decide whether to carry an umbrella. On any day of a given season he sees the forecast, if it says "rain" he will always carry an umbrella, and if it says "no rain," he will not carry an umbrella. Are the events "Victor is carrying an umbrella," and "The forecast is no rain" independent?  Give answer as 1 if independent else give 0 as answer..
questions.questionHtml:
The probability of Victor missing the morning forecast is equal to 0.2 on any day in the year. If he misses the forecast, Victor will flip a fair coin to decide whether to carry an umbrella. On any day of a given season he sees the forecast, if it says "rain" he will always carry an umbrella, and if it says "no rain," he will not carry an umbrella. Are the events "Victor is carrying an umbrella," and "The forecast is no rain" independent? 

Give answer as 1 if independent else give 0 as answer..
questions.explanation: Let $C$ be the event that Victor is carrying an umbrella. Let $D$ be the event that the forecast is no rain. The tree diagram in this case is: $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{P}(D) & =1-p \\ \mathbf{P}(C) & =(0.8) p+(0.2)(0.5)=0.8 p+0.1 \\ \mathbf{P}(C \mid D) & =(0.8)(0)+(0.2)(0.5)=0.1 \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $\mathbf{P}(C)=\mathbf{P}(C \mid D)$ if and only if $p=0$. However, $p$ can only be 0.7 or 0.2 , which implies the events $C$ and $D$ can never be independent. $15$ balls are placed independently and uniformly at random into $15$ bins numbered from $1$ to $15.$ The probability that a ball ends up in a particular bin is $\frac{1}{15}.$

What is the probability that the first $5$ balls go into different bins, conditioned on the event that first four balls are in different bins?

questions.questionText: A cloth bag labeled $X$ contains two apples, bag $Y$ contains two oranges and bag $Z$ one apple and one orange. You pick a bag at random and then remove one fruit from that bag at random. Suppose you removed an apple. What is the probability that the fruit remaining in the bag is also an apple? Justify.
questions.questionHtml: A cloth bag labeled $X$ contains two apples, bag $Y$ contains two oranges and bag $Z$ one apple and one orange. You pick a bag at random and then remove one fruit from that bag at random. Suppose you removed an apple. What is the probability that the fruit remaining in the bag is also an apple? Justify.
questions.explanation: Let following events be defined: $A$: the second fruit remaining is an apple $E$: the first fruit drawn is an apple We want to compute: $ \Pr(A \mid E) = \text{Probability that the remaining fruit is an apple given that the first fruit drawn is an apple} $ Picking each bag is equally likely so probability = $1/3$ Total probability of drawing apple: From X: $1/3 \cdot 2/2 = 1/3$ From Y: $1/3 \cdot 0/2=0$ From Z: $1/3 \cdot 1/2 = 1/6$ So, $$ \Pr(E) = 1/3 + 0 + 1/6 = 1/2 $$  $\Pr(A \cap E)$ is the  probability that the first fruit is an apple, and the second fruit is also an apple This is possible only if you picked $\textbf{Bag X}$ (only bag with two apples — Y has no apples and Z has only one apple) So, $$ \Pr(A \cap E) = \Pr(\text{picked Bag X and drew an apple}) = \frac{1}{3} \cdot 1 = \frac{1}{3} $$ Then: $$ \Pr(A \mid E) = \frac{\Pr(A \cap E)}{\Pr(E)} = \frac{1/3}{1/2} = \boxed{\frac{2}{3}} $$ Abhishek-1011 answered Jul 9, 2025 Abhishek-1011 comment Share Follow 0 reply P

questions.title: TIFR CSE 2025 | Part A | Question: 12
questions.excerpt: Consider a coin which has probability $p$ of coming up heads when tossed. Assume that $0<p<10 < p < 10<p<1$. A trial is performed by repeatedly tossing the coin until the...
questions.questionText: Consider a coin which has probability $p$ of coming up heads when tossed. Assume that $0<p<10 < p < 10<p<1$. A trial is performed by repeatedly tossing the coin until the first time it shows a head: the number of tosses made is then called the value of the trial. (Thus, if a trial results in tosses “tails”, “tails”, “heads”, then its value is $3$) An experiment is a sequence of $n$ independent trials. Akhil and Bela each perform an experiment, as defined above, with the coin. Akhil defines the value $A$ of his experiment to be the maximum of the values of the $n$ trials in his experiment, while Bela defines the value $B$ of her experiment to be the average of the value of the $n$ trials in her experiment. Which of the following is correct? (Here, for any random variable $X, E[X]$ denotes the expectation of $X$.) $E[A]$ is a strictly increasing function of $n$ while $E[B]$ does not depend upon $n$. $E[A]$ is a non-constant function of $n$, but it is not strictly increasing, while $E[B]$ does not depend upon $n$. $E[A]$ and $E[B]$ are both strictly increasing functions of $n$. $E[A]$ is a non-decreasing function of $n$ while $E[B]$ is a strictly decreasing function of $n$. Neither $E[A]$ nor $E[B]$ depends upon $n$.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a coin which has probability $p$ of coming up heads when tossed. Assume that $0<p<10 < p < 10<p<1$. A trial is performed by repeatedly tossing the coin until the first time it shows a head: the number of tosses made is then called the value of the trial. (Thus, if a trial results in tosses “tails”, “tails”, “heads”, then its value is $3$) An experiment is a sequence of $n$ independent trials.

Akhil and Bela each perform an experiment, as defined above, with the coin. Akhil defines the value $A$ of his experiment to be the maximum of the values of the $n$ trials in his experiment, while Bela defines the value $B$ of her experiment to be the average of the value of the $n$ trials in her experiment. Which of the following is correct? (Here, for any random variable $X, E[X]$ denotes the expectation of $X$.)

  1. $E[A]$ is a strictly increasing function of $n$ while $E[B]$ does not depend upon $n$.
  2. $E[A]$ is a non-constant function of $n$, but it is not strictly increasing, while $E[B]$ does not depend upon $n$.
  3. $E[A]$ and $E[B]$ are both strictly increasing functions of $n$.
  4. $E[A]$ is a non-decreasing function of $n$ while $E[B]$ is a strictly decreasing function of $n$.
  5. Neither $E[A]$ nor $E[B]$ depends upon $n$.

options.label: A
options.text: $E[A]$ is a strictly increasing function of $n$ while $E[B]$ does not depend upon $n$.

options.label: B
options.text: $E[A]$ is a non-constant function of $n$, but it is not strictly increasing, while $E[B]$ does not depend upon $n$.

options.label: C
options.text: $E[A]$ and $E[B]$ are both strictly increasing functions of $n$.

options.label: D
options.text: $E[A]$ is a non-decreasing function of $n$ while $E[B]$ is a strictly decreasing function of $n$.

questions.explanation: Let $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ be the values of the $n$ trials, Bela's value is : $$ B_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i $$ We want the expectation $\mathbb{E}[B_n]$. \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[B_n] &= \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i\right] \\ &= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{E}[X_i] \end{align*} Since each $X_i \sim \text{Geometric}(p)$, we know: $$ \mathbb{E}[X_i] = \frac{1}{p} \quad \text{for all } i $$ Therefore: $$ \mathbb{E}[B_n] = \frac{1}{n} \cdot n \cdot \frac{1}{p} = \frac{1}{p} $$ $$ \boxed{ \mathbb{E}[B_n] = \frac{1}{p} } $$ Hence, Bela’s expected value does not depend on $n$. Akhil's value is $$A_n = \max(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)$$  Then expectation of $A_n$ is,: \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}[A_n] = \sum_{k = 1}^{\infty} k \cdot P(A_n = k) \tag{i} \end{equation} So we first need tofind $P(A_n = k)$. This can be found as: \begin{equation} P(A_n = k) = P(A_n \leq k) - P(A_n \leq k - 1) \tag{ii} \end{equation} So lets find $P(A_n \leq k)$ . Since

questions.explanation: click here $\text{Answer: A}$ SilentClimber answered Feb 21 SilentClimber comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes This problem is a classic application of conditional probability and the Binomial Distribution . We are looking for $P(Z = 3 \mid B = 2)$, where $B$ is the number of heads Bob gets. Alice's Tossing ($Z$): Alice tosses a coin 4 times. $Z \sim \text{Binomial}(n=4, p=1/2)$. Bob's Tossing ($B$): Bob tosses the coin $Z$ times. Given $Z = k$, Bob's heads $B \sim \text{Binomial}(n=k, p=1/2)$. Use Bayes' Theorem To find $P(Z = 3 \mid B = 2)$, we use the formula: $$P(Z = 3 \mid B = 2) = \frac{P(B = 2 \mid Z = 3) \cdot P(Z = 3)}{P(B = 2)}$$ First, let's find the individual probabilities for $Z$: $P(Z=2) = \binom{4}{2} (\frac{1}{2})^4 = \frac{6}{16}$ $P(Z=3) = \binom{4}{3} (\frac{1}{2})^4 = \frac{4}{16}$ $P(Z=4) = \binom{4}{4} (\frac{1}{2})^4 = \frac{1}{16}$ (Note: Bob cannot get 2 heads if $Z < 2$, so we ignore $Z=0$ and $Z=1$.) questions.explanation: (B) SOURAV 1 answered Jun 18, 2025 SOURAV 1 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes OPTION B is correct answer. So to statisfy the given conditions ie the experiment  should stop exactly after eight tosses : we have two cases case1: we get 7 heads and then 1 tail in a sequence : the probability for this will be 2/6561 case 2 : we get 7 tail and then 1 head in a sequence : the probability for this will be 128/6561 so the expected probability is the sum of these two , therefore the probability that the experiment  should stop exactly after eight tosses is 130/6561

questions.explanation: The total number of possible speaking orders for \( 8 \) distinct individuals is,\[8!\]Favorable Orders (\( P \rightarrow Q \rightarrow R \) (only 1 way)), 3 positions out of \( 8 \) for \( P, Q, R \),\[\binom{8}{3}\]Arranging the remaining 5 speakers,\[5!\]The number of favorable orders is,\[\binom{8}{3} \times 5!\]\[\text{Probability} = \frac{\binom{8}{3} \times 5!}{8!} = \frac{\frac{8!}{3!5!} \times 5!}{8!} = \frac{1}{3!} = \frac{1}{6}\] BhavdeepSinghNijhawa answered Mar 27, 2025 BhavdeepSinghNijhawa comment Share Follow See 1 comment 1 1 comment reply Honey badger commented Mar 28, 2025 reply Follow flag if there would have more favourable orderes e.g. p->r->q , we just have to multiply by 2? 0 0 reply Share Please log in or register to add a comment. A certain brand of software claims that it can detect $99 \%$ of spam emails, and the probability for a false positive (a non-spam email detected as spam) is $5 \%$. Now if an email is detected as spam, then what is the probability that it is in fact a non-spam email? $1 / 104$ $95 / 104$ $5 / 104$ $99 / 104$
questions.questionHtml:
It is estimated that $50 \%$ of emails are spam emails. Some software has been applied to filter these spam emails before they reach your inbox. A certain brand of software claims that it can detect $99 \%$ of spam emails, and the probability for a false positive (a non-spam email detected as spam) is $5 \%$.

Now if an email is detected as spam, then what is the probability that it is in fact a non-spam email?

  1. $1 / 104$
     
  2. $95 / 104$
     
  3. $5 / 104$
     
  4. $99 / 104$
questions.explanation: Define events $A=$ event that an email is detected as spam, $B=$ event that an email is a spam, $B^{c}=$ event that an email is not spam. We know $P(B)=P\left(B^{c}\right)=.5, \quad P(A \mid B)=0.99, \quad P\left(A \mid B^{c}\right)=0.05$. Hence by Bayes's formula, we have $$ \begin{aligned} P\left(B^{c} \mid A\right) &=\frac{P\left(A \mid B^{c}\right) P\left(B^{c}\right)}{P(A \mid B) P(B)+P\left(A \mid B^{c}\right) P\left(B^{c}\right)} \\ &=\frac{0.05 \times 0.5}{0.05 \times 0.5+0.99 \times 0.5} \\ &=\frac{5}{104} . \end{aligned} $$                                                                             OR   . questions.explanation: This is just a version of the Law of Total Expectaion.  \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X | Y]]  = \mathbb{E}[X]  \end{align*} Hence, answer is (C) Proof: \begin{align*} \\ \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X | Y]] &= \sum_y P(Y = y) \mathbb{E}[X | Y = y] \quad \text{(LOTUS, with } g(Y) = \mathbb{E}[X | Y] \text{)} \\ &= \sum_y P(Y = y) \sum_x x P(X = x | Y = y) \quad \text{(Definition of Conditional Expectation)} \\ &= \sum_y \sum_x x P(X = x | Y = y) P(Y = y) \\ &= \sum_x \sum_y x P(X = x, Y = y) \quad \text{(Chain Rule)} \\ &= \sum_x x \sum_y P(X = x, Y = y) \quad \text{(Switch Order of Summation)} \\ &= \sum_x x P(X = x) \quad \text{(Marginalization)} \\ &= \mathbb{E}[X] \end{align*} bruh seal answered Feb 28, 2025 bruh seal comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes By the law of total expectation, \[ \mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_{y} \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y] \, \mathbb{P}(Y = y). \] We know that the conditional e

questions.explanation: Using the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the Exponential Random Variable with parameter \(\lambda\): \[ F_X(x) = \begin{cases} 1 - e^{-\lambda x}, & x \geq 0 \\ 0, & x < 0 \end{cases} \] We want to find \(\lambda\) given that: \[ \begin{aligned} P(X \geq 2) &= 1 - P(X < 2) \\ &= 1 - F_X(2) \\ &= 1 - (1 - e^{-2\lambda}) \\ &= e^{-2\lambda} \end{aligned} \] This probability value is already given: \[ e^{-2\lambda} = 0.25 \] Taking the natural logarithm on both sides: \[ \begin{aligned} -2\lambda \ln e &= \ln \left(\frac{1}{4}\right) \\ -2\lambda &= \ln 1 - \ln 4 \\ -2\lambda &= -\ln 4 = -\ln 2^2 = -2 \ln 2 \\ \lambda &= \ln 2 \end{aligned} \] bruh seal answered Feb 28, 2025 • edited Feb 28, 2025 by bruh seal bruh seal comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 3 3 votes ``````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````` I have used (log base e) here as [natura

questions.questionText: ​​​​Consider a coin-toss experiment where the probability of head showing up is $p$. In the $i^{\text {th }}$ coin toss, let $X_{i}=1$ if head appears, and $X_{i}=0$ if tail appears. Consider \[ \widehat{p}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i} \] where $n$ is the total number of independent coin tosses. Which of the following statements is/are correct? $E[\widehat{p}]=p$ $E[\widehat{p}]=\dfrac{p}{n}$ As $n$ increases, variance of $\widehat{p}$ decreases Variance of $\widehat{p}$ does not depend on $n$
questions.questionHtml:
​​​​Consider a coin-toss experiment where the probability of head showing up is $p$. In the $i^{\text {th }}$ coin toss, let $X_{i}=1$ if head appears, and $X_{i}=0$ if tail appears. Consider
\[
\widehat{p}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i}
\]
where $n$ is the total number of independent coin tosses.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  1. $E[\widehat{p}]=p$
  2. $E[\widehat{p}]=\dfrac{p}{n}$
  3. As $n$ increases, variance of $\widehat{p}$ decreases
  4. Variance of $\widehat{p}$ does not depend on $n$

options.label: D
options.text: Variance of $\widehat{p}$ does not depend on $n$

questions.explanation: $\hat{p} = \frac{1}{n} (X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n)$ $E[\hat{p}] = E[\frac{1}{n} (X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n)$] $= \frac{1}{n} E[(X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n)$] $= \frac{1}{n} (np)$  {Binomial Distribution} $ E[\hat{p}] = p $ $Var[\hat{p}] = Var[\frac{1}{n} (X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n)$] $ = \frac{1}{n^2} Var[ (X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n)$] $= \frac{1}{(n^2)} (np(1-p))$  {Binomial Distribution} $= \frac{p(1-p)}{n}$ $Var[\hat{p}]$  is inversely proportional to n Correct Answer A, C

We can rewrite the first equation as: $$\alpha + \beta = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 2\alpha \beta$$ So we have two cases: Case 1:  $\alpha \beta = 0$ \begin{gathered}   \alpha + \beta = (\alpha + \beta)^2 \\   \implies \alpha + \beta = 0 \; \text{or} \; 1 \end{gathered} For $\alpha \beta = 0$ and $\alpha + \beta = 0$, we get $\alpha = \beta = 0$. questions.explanation: Solution: Rs 4500 Explanation: For each 1 ≤ i ≤ 10 the probability that the empty box is labelled i, is 1/10. questions.questionText: A prominent newspaper conducted a survey among a carefully chosen sample of $1,00,000$ voters under the age of $25$. A randomly chosen subset of $60 \%$ of this sample were asked the following question: "Have you ever voted in a general election?" The remaining $40 \%$ were asked the following, different question: "Is it true that you have never voted in a general election?" The editor in charge of collating the data from the survey, accidentally deleted some of the contents of the survey database. The only information that survived this mishap was that a total of $54,000$ respondents replied Yes to the question that they got. Specifically, it is not known how many of these Yes answers correspond to the first question, and how many to the second. Assume that the sampling was done properly and that the respondents answered truthfully. What estimate can we derive from just the total number of YES answers, about the percentage of voters under the age of $25$ that have voted in some general election? At most $30 \%$. More than $30 \%$, but less than $60 \%$. At least $60 \%$, but less than $75 \%$. No such estimate can be drawn from just the total number of Yes answers.

A prominent newspaper conducted a survey among a carefully chosen sample of $1,00,000$ voters under the age of $25$. A randomly chosen subset of $60 \%$ of this sample were asked the following question: "Have you ever voted in a general election?" The remaining $40 \%$ were asked the following, different question: "Is it true that you have never voted in a general election?"
The editor in charge of collating the data from the survey, accidentally deleted some of the contents of the survey database. The only information that survived this mishap was that a total of $54,000$ respondents replied Yes to the question that they got. Specifically, it is not known how many of these Yes answers correspond to the first question, and how many to the second.
Assume that the sampling was done properly and that the respondents answered truthfully. What estimate can we derive from just the total number of YES answers, about the percentage of voters under the age of $25$ that have voted in some general election?

  1. At most $30 \%$.
  2. More than $30 \%$, but less than $60 \%$.
  3. At least $60 \%$, but less than $75 \%$.
  4. No such estimate can be drawn from just the total number of Yes answers.

options.label: D
options.text: No such estimate can be drawn from just the total number of Yes answers.

questions.explanation: For finding the maximum number of voters who told YES for the 1st question (that is, they have voted in any of the general elections beforehand), we need to assume that all the YES answers remaining, i.e. 54,000 answers are given by the 60% voters, who were asked the 1st question... Because YES for the 2nd question means that the voting hasn't been doneby the person...{NO in actual to voting} So, calculating the percentage.. We'll find that (54,000) * 100 / 1,00,000 = 5.4% percent wise ranges from [0, 5.4] which is lesser than 30, so, at most 30 must be the answer.. Option A is correct.

questions.questionText: Two friends $A$ and $B$ are playing a coin flipping game with a fair coin, based on the following rules: When $A$ flips the coin               - If it is heads then $A$ wins and the game ends.               - If it is tails then $B$ gets to flip the coin. When $B$ flips the coin             - If it is heads then $B$ wins and the game ends.             - If it is tails then $A$ gets to flip the coin.             - The flipping continues till someone gets heads. Suppose $A$ is the first player to flip the coin. What is the probability that $A$ will win the game.
questions.questionHtml:
Two friends $A$ and $B$ are playing a coin flipping game with a fair coin, based on the following rules:

  • When $A$ flips the coin

              - If it is heads then $A$ wins and the game ends.
              - If it is tails then $B$ gets to flip the coin.

  • When $B$ flips the coin

            - If it is heads then $B$ wins and the game ends.
            - If it is tails then $A$ gets to flip the coin.
            - The flipping continues till someone gets heads.

Suppose $A$ is the first player to flip the coin. What is the probability that $A$ will win the game.
questions.explanation: Let start by analyzing the structure of the game.  The coin is fair, so \(P(H)=P(T)=0.5\).  \(A\) flips the coin first, so, in the first trial, \(A\) winning the game has probability \(0.5\). If \(A\) loses, i.e., the outcome of the first toss was a tails, then in the next trial, \(B\) has to lose , to ensure \(A\) even has a chance of winning.  So, the probability of \(B\) losing the second game given \(A\) has lost the first game has a probability \(0.5\times0.5=(0.5)^2\). Now in the third trial, if the outcome is heads, then \(A\) wins, which has a probability of \((0.5)^2\times 0.5=(0.5)^3\). If \(A\) loses in the third trial, then like before \(B\) has to lose the next game.  This pattern goes on until \(A\) wins, So, probabiliy of \(A\) winning the game is the sum, \[P(A \text{ wins})=0.5+(0.5)^3+(0.5)^5+\ldots=\sum_{i=0}^\infty(0.5)^{2i+1}\] Solving the infinite geometric series sum we get, \[P(A\text{ wins})=\frac{0.5}{1-(0.5)^2}=\frac{2}{3}\] I highly reco

questions.explanation: Rohit wins if and only if the first two tosses give Heads, there's no other possibility. questions.explanation: There are only two possible perfect squares 4 and 9. The cases corresponding to sum being equal to 4 are (1, 3), (2, 2), and (3, 1), where the first entry represents the number on the first die and second number on the second die, totaling 3, And that for the sum being equal to 9 we have (3, 6), (4, 5), (5, 4), and (6, 3), totaling 4. questions.questionText: A student appears for a quiz consisting of only true-false type questions and answers all the questions.  The student knows the answers of some questions and guesses the answers for the remaining questions.  Whenever the student knows the answer of a question, he gives the correct answer.  Assume that the probability of the student giving the correct answer for a question, given that he has guessed it, is 1/2 Also assume that the probability of the answer for a question being guessed, given that the student’s answer is correct, is 1/6 Then the probability that the student knows the answer of a randomly chosen question is       (A)  1/12 (B)  1/7 (C)  5/7 (D)  5/12
questions.questionHtml:
A student appears for a quiz consisting of only true-false type questions and answers all the questions.  The student knows the answers of some questions and guesses the answers for the remaining questions.  Whenever the student knows the answer of a question, he gives the correct answer.  Assume that the probability of the student giving the correct answer for a question, given that he has guessed it, is 1/2 Also assume that the probability of the answer for a question being guessed, given that the student’s answer is correct, is 1/6 Then the probability that the student knows the answer of a randomly chosen question is      

(A)  1/12 (B)  1/7 (C)  5/7 (D)  5/12
questions.explanation: Let $A$ be the event that the question is known and $B$ be the event that the Question is unkown, so that he need to guess. Let $P(A)=p$ and $P(B)=1-p$, as these are only two events for the experiment. Let $C$ be the event that the answer is correct. The we know the following info, $P(C|A)=1$, $P(C|B)=1/2$, and $P(B|C)=1/6$. We could find the probability that the the question is NOT unkown (or he knows the question) given that the answer is correct , that is, $P(B^c|C)= 1-1/6= 5/6=P(A|C)$. We know from the Baye's formulaa - $P(C|A)=P(A|C)P(C)/P(A)$ $1=(5/6p)P(C)$      (1) and $P(C|B)=P(B|C)P(C)/P(B)$ $1/2=(1/6(1-p))P(C)$     (2) Take the ratio of eqn., 1 and 2 to get - $2p=5(1-p)$ $p=5/7$. Option C is correct.

questions.questionText: Suppose X and Y are two independent random variables, such that X has probability mass function $P(X=x) = (1/3)(2/3)^{x-1}$  for integers $x \geq 1$, and Y has probability mass function $P(Y=y) = (2/5)(3/5)^{y-1}$ for integers $y \geq 1$. Find $\mathit{\textbf{P(X=Y)}}$. A) 1/9            B) 2/9            C) 1/3            D) 1/2
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose X and Y are two independent random variables,

such that X has probability mass function $P(X=x) = (1/3)(2/3)^{x-1}$  for integers $x \geq 1$,

and Y has probability mass function $P(Y=y) = (2/5)(3/5)^{y-1}$ for integers $y \geq 1$.

Find $\mathit{\textbf{P(X=Y)}}$.

 

A) 1/9            B) 2/9            C) 1/3            D) 1/2
questions.explanation: $X=m$ is an event which means the r.v $X$ takes the value $x$, $X=Y$ means $X=m$ and $Y=m$ for all $m$. Since $P(X=m,Y=m)=P(X=m)P(Y=m)$ [indp. of events], the required probability is -  \( \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} P(X=m)P(Y=m) =\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}(1/3)(2/3)^{m-1}(2/5)(3/5)^{m-1}=(2/15)\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}(6/15)^{m-1}\) The sum of the GP is \(\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}(6/15)^{m-1}=1/(1-(6/15))=15/9\), hence the reqd probability is $(15/9)(2/15)=2/9$. Option B is correct

questions.questionText: Given random variables $X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots$ which are independent and identically distributed (iid) random variables, each $X_{j}$ has the same Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) $F_{X}(x)$. i.e., $P\left(X_{i} \leq x\right)=F_{X}(x)$ for all $X_{i}$. Consider $L_{n}=\min \left(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}\right)$. Which of the following is the correct expression for $F_{L_{n}}(l)$ ? $F_{L_{n}}(l)=1-\left(1-F_{X}(l)\right)^{n}$ $F_{L_{n}}(l)=n F_{X}(l)\left(1-F_{X}(l)\right)^{n-1}$ $F_{L_{n}}(l)=n\left(F_{X}(l)\right)^{n-1}$ $F_{L_{n}}(l)=\left(F_{X}(l)\right)^{n}$
questions.questionHtml:
Given random variables $X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots$ which are independent and identically distributed (iid) random variables, each $X_{j}$ has the same Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) $F_{X}(x)$.
i.e., $P\left(X_{i} \leq x\right)=F_{X}(x)$ for all $X_{i}$.
Consider $L_{n}=\min \left(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}\right)$.
Which of the following is the correct expression for $F_{L_{n}}(l)$ ?

  1. $F_{L_{n}}(l)=1-\left(1-F_{X}(l)\right)^{n}$
     
  2. $F_{L_{n}}(l)=n F_{X}(l)\left(1-F_{X}(l)\right)^{n-1}$
     
  3. $F_{L_{n}}(l)=n\left(F_{X}(l)\right)^{n-1}$
     
  4. $F_{L_{n}}(l)=\left(F_{X}(l)\right)^{n}$
questions.explanation: $F_{L_{n}}(l)=P\left(L_{n} \leq l\right)$ Since $L_{n}=\min \left(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}\right), L_{n} \leq l$ if and only if at least one of the $X_{i}$ is less than or equal to $l$. The complement of this event is that all $X_{i}$ are greater than $l$ : $P\left(L_{n} \leq l\right)=1-P\left(L_{n}>l\right)$ $P\left(L_{n}>l\right)=P\left(\min \left(X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}\right)>l\right)$ This occurs if and only if all $X_{i}$ are greater than $l$ : $P\left(L_{n}>l\right)=P\left(X_{1}>l\right) \cdot P\left(X_{2}>l\right) \cdot \ldots \cdot P\left(X_{n}>l\right)$ Since the $X_{i}$ are iid with CDF $F_{X}(x)$, we have: $P\left(X_{i}>l\right)=1-P\left(X_{i} \leq l\right)=1-F_{X}(l)$ Thus: $P\left(L_{n}>l\right)=\left(1-F_{X}(l)\right)^{n}$ So: $P\left(L_{n} \leq l\right)=1-\left(1-F_{X}(l)\right)^{n}$ Therefore, the CDF of $L_{n}$ is: $F_{L_{n}}(l)=1-\left(1-F_{X}(l)\right)^{n}$ The correct expression for $F_{L_{n}}(l)$ is: A) $F_{L_{n}}(l)=1-\left(1-F_{X}(l)\right)^

Let $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ be two independent Bernoulli random variables with the probability of success $p$, where $X_{i}=0$ with probability $1-p$ and $X_{i}=1$ with probability $p$ for $i=1,2$. Define a random variable $Y=X_{1}+X_{2}$. Therefore, $Y$ follows a Binomial Distribution with $n=2$ trials.

What is $E\left[Y \mid X_{1}=1\right]$ ?

  1. $p$
     
  2. $1-p$
     
  3. $1+p$
     
  4. $2-p$
questions.explanation: Given $X_{1}=1$, $E\left[Y \mid X_{1}=1\right]=E\left[X_{1}+X_{2} \mid X_{1}=1\right]=E\left[X_{1} \mid X_{1}=1\right]+E\left[X_{2} \mid X_{1}=1\right]$ By the properties of conditional expectation and independence of $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ : $E\left[Y \mid X_{1}=1\right]=1+E\left[X_{2}\right]$ Since $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ are independent Bernoulli random variables with success probability $p$, $E\left[X_{2}\right]=p$ Therefore, $E\left[Y \mid X_{1}=1\right]=1+p$ So, the answer is $1+p$. questions.questionText: Consider the following statements regarding properties of a continuous random variable $X$ that is always positive. Identify the true statements: $\mathrm{E}\left[X^{k}\right]=\int_{0}^{\infty} k x^{k-1} \mathrm{P}(X>x) d x$, for $k \geq 1$. $\mathrm{E}\left[X^{k}\right]=\int_{0}^{\infty} k x^{k} \mathrm{P}(X>x) d x$, for $k \geq 1$. $\mathrm{E}\left[X^{2}\right]<(\mathrm{E}[X])^{2}$. $\mathrm{E}\left[X^{2}\right] \geq(\mathrm{E}[X])^{2}$.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following statements regarding properties of a continuous random variable $X$ that is always positive. Identify the true statements:

  1. $\mathrm{E}\left[X^{k}\right]=\int_{0}^{\infty} k x^{k-1} \mathrm{P}(X>x) d x$, for $k \geq 1$.
     
  2. $\mathrm{E}\left[X^{k}\right]=\int_{0}^{\infty} k x^{k} \mathrm{P}(X>x) d x$, for $k \geq 1$.
     
  3. $\mathrm{E}\left[X^{2}\right]<(\mathrm{E}[X])^{2}$.
     
  4. $\mathrm{E}\left[X^{2}\right] \geq(\mathrm{E}[X])^{2}$.
questions.explanation: 1. TRUE or FALSE? If $X$ is a continuous random variable that is always positive, then $\mathrm{E}\left[X^{k}\right]=\int_{0}^{\infty} k x^{k-1} \mathrm{P}(X>x) d x$, for $k \geq 1$. Solution: True. Here's the proof. $$ \begin{aligned} \int_{0}^{\infty} k x^{k-1} \mathrm{P}(X>x) d x & =\int_{0}^{\infty} k x^{k-1} \int_{x}^{\infty} f(t) d t d x \\ & =\int_{0}^{\infty} f(t) \int_{0}^{t} k x^{k-1} d x d t \\ & =\int_{0}^{\infty} f(t) t^{k} d t \\ & =\mathrm{E}\left[X^{k}\right] . \diamond \end{aligned} $$ 3. TRUE or FALSE? $\mathrm{E}\left[X^{2}\right] \geq(\mathrm{E}[X])^{2}$. Solution: TRUE, since $0 \leq \operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathrm{E}\left[X^{2}\right]-(\mathrm{E}[X])^{2}$. questions.questionHtml:
Let $U$ be uniformly distributed over $(0,1)$ and $V$ be uniformly distributed over $(0, U)$. Using the law of total expectation, what is $E[V]$ ?
 

  1. $\frac{1}{8}$
     
  2. $\frac{1}{4}$
     
  3. $\frac{1}{2}$
     
  4. $1$
questions.explanation: Given $U \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)$ and $V \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0, U)$ : $E[V \mid U=u]=\frac{u}{2}$, because $V$ given $U=u$ is uniformly distributed on $(0, u)$ with mean $\frac{u}{2}$. Using the law of total expectation: $E[V]=E[E[V \mid U]]=E\left[\frac{U}{2}\right]=\frac{1}{2} E[U]$ Since $U \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0,1), E[U]=\frac{1}{2}$. Therefore, $E[V]=\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{4}$ Thus, $E[V]=\frac{1}{4}$. questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following represents $\mathbb{E}\left(X^{3} \mid Y=y\right)$, given the joint density of $X$ and $Y$ ?
$$
f(x, y)= \begin{cases}\frac{e^{-y}}{y} & \text { if } 0<x<y, 0<y<\infty \\\\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}
$$

  1. $\frac{y^{3}}{4}$
     
  2. $\frac{y^{3}}{3}$
     
  3. $\frac{y^{4}}{4}$
     
  4. $\frac{y^{2}}{2}$
questions.explanation: Solution: We have $$ f_{Y}(y)=\int_{0}^{y} \frac{e^{-y}}{y} d x=e^{-y} $$ so that $$ f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc} \frac{1}{y} & x \in(0, y) \\ 0 & \text { otherwise } \end{array}\right. $$ We conclude that $$ \mathbb{E}\left(X^{3} \mid Y=y\right)=\int_{0}^{y} \frac{x^{3}}{y} d x=\frac{y^{3}}{4} $$ GO Classes answered Jun 19, 2024 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionHtml:
Let the CDF of a continuous random variable $Y$ be
$$
F(y)= \begin{cases}0, & y \leq 0 \\\\ \frac{y}{8}, & 0<y<2 \\\\ \frac{y^{2}}{16}, & 2 \leq y<4 \\\\ 1, & y \geq 4\end{cases}
$$Find $P(Y \geq 1 \mid Y \leq 3)$.

  1. $\frac{7}{9}$
     
  2. $\frac{9}{7}$
     
  3. $\frac{7}{16}$
     
  4. $\frac{16}{7}$
questions.explanation: We have, $$ \begin{aligned} P(1 \leq Y \leq 3) & =P(1<Y \leq 3) \quad \text { (Y is continuous) } \\ & =F(3)-F(1) \\ & =\frac{3^{2}}{16}-\frac{1}{8}=\frac{9}{16}-\frac{2}{16}=\frac{7}{16} . \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ P(Y \geq 1 \mid Y \leq 3)=\frac{P(1 \leq Y \leq 3)}{P(Y \leq 3)}=\frac{7 / 16}{9 / 16}=\frac{7}{9} $$ GO Classes answered Jun 19, 2024 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Let $X_{i}, i=1, \ldots, 4$ be independent Bernoulli r.v.s each with mean $p=0.1$ and let $S=\sum_{i=1}^{4} X_{i}$. Then, $\mathbb{E}\left(X_{1} \mid S=2\right)=0.1$. $\mathbb{E}\left(X_{1} \mid S=2\right)=0.5$. $\mathbb{E}\left(X_{1} \mid S=2\right)=0.25$. $\mathbb{E}\left(X_{1} \mid S=2\right)=0.75$.
questions.questionHtml:
Let $X_{i}, i=1, \ldots, 4$ be independent Bernoulli r.v.s each with mean $p=0.1$ and let $S=\sum_{i=1}^{4} X_{i}$. Then,

  1. $\mathbb{E}\left(X_{1} \mid S=2\right)=0.1$.
     
  2. $\mathbb{E}\left(X_{1} \mid S=2\right)=0.5$.
     
  3. $\mathbb{E}\left(X_{1} \mid S=2\right)=0.25$.
     
  4. $\mathbb{E}\left(X_{1} \mid S=2\right)=0.75$.
questions.explanation: Solution: (b) since $$ \mathbb{E}\left(X_1 \mid S=2\right)=\mathbb{P}\left(X_1=1 \mid S=2\right)=\frac{\mathbb{P}\left(X_1=1, S=2\right)}{\mathbb{P}(S=2)}=\frac{p \times 3 p(1-p)^2}{\binom{4}{2} p^2(1-p)^2}=0.5 \text {. } $$ (Note that $\binom{4}{2} p^2(1-p)^2$ is the probability of seeing 2 heads out of 4 tosses, and $\binom{3}{1} p(1-p)^2$ is the probability of seeing 1 head in the last 3 tosses.) questions.questionText: Suppose that $X$ is a random variable with support $\{1,2\}$ and $Y$ is a random variable with support $\{0,1\}$ where $X$ and $Y$ have the following joint distribution: $$ \begin{aligned} & p_{X Y}(1,0)=0.25 \\ & p_{X Y}(1,1)=0.25 \\ & p_{X Y}(2,0)=0.25 \\ & p_{X Y}(2,1)=0.25 \end{aligned} $$ What is the covariance between $X$ and $Y$ ? $0.25$ $0.5$ $0$ $1$
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose that $X$ is a random variable with support $\{1,2\}$ and $Y$ is a random variable with support $\{0,1\}$ where $X$ and $Y$ have the following joint distribution:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& p_{X Y}(1,0)=0.25 \\
& p_{X Y}(1,1)=0.25 \\
& p_{X Y}(2,0)=0.25 \\
& p_{X Y}(2,1)=0.25
\end{aligned}
$$
What is the covariance between $X$ and $Y$ ?

  1. $0.25$
     
  2. $0.5$
     
  3. $0$
     
  4. $1$
questions.explanation: The marginal PMFs of \(X\) and \(Y\) are as follows: \[ \begin{aligned} & p_X(1) = p_{XY}(1,0) + p_{XY}(1,1) = 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5 \\ & p_X(2) = p_{XY}(2,0) + p_{XY}(2,1) = 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5 \\ & p_Y(0) = p_{XY}(1,0) + p_{XY}(2,0) = 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5 \\ & p_Y(1) = p_{XY}(1,1) + p_{XY}(2,1) = 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5 \end{aligned} \] First, from the marginal distributions, we find: \[ E[X] = 1.5 \] \[ E[Y] = 0.5 \] \[ E[X]E[Y] = 1.5 \times 0.5 = 0.75 \] Second, we calculate \(E[XY]\): \[ \begin{aligned} E[XY] &= (1 \cdot 0) \cdot 0.25 + (2 \cdot 0) \cdot 0.25 + (1 \cdot 1) \cdot 0.25 + (2 \cdot 1) \cdot 0.25 \\ &= 0 + 0 + 0.25 + 0.5 = 0.75 \end{aligned} \] Finally, we compute the covariance: \[ \operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y] = 0.75 - 0.75 = 0 \] Alternatively, one could observe from the table that \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent. Since independence implies zero covariance, this conclusion can be reached without further calculations. Sachin Mittal 1 answered

questions.questionText: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with joint pdf $$ f(x, y)= \begin{cases}c x^{2} y(1+y) & \text { if } 0 \leq x \leq 3 \text { and } 0 \leq y \leq 3 \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases} $$ Find the marginal cdf $F_{X}(a)$ for $a$ between $0$ and $3$. $F_{X}(a)=\frac{a^{3}}{27}$ $F_{X}(a)=\frac{a^{3}}{18}$ $F_{X}(a)=\frac{a^{3}}{9}$ $F_{X}(a)=\frac{a^{3}}{54}$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with joint pdf
$$
f(x, y)= \begin{cases}c x^{2} y(1+y) & \text { if } 0 \leq x \leq 3 \text { and } 0 \leq y \leq 3 \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}
$$
Find the marginal cdf $F_{X}(a)$ for $a$ between $0$ and $3$.

  1. $F_{X}(a)=\frac{a^{3}}{27}$
     
  2. $F_{X}(a)=\frac{a^{3}}{18}$
     
  3. $F_{X}(a)=\frac{a^{3}}{9}$
     
  4. $F_{X}(a)=\frac{a^{3}}{54}$
questions.explanation: The total probability must sum to 1, so we have: $$ 1 = \int_0^3 \int_0^3 f(x, y) \, dy \, dx = \int_0^3 \int_0^3 c \left(x^2 y + x^2 y^2\right) \, dy \, dx = c \cdot \frac{243}{2}. $$ (Here we omitted the arithmetic details of the integration.) Therefore, \( c = \frac{2}{243} \). For \( 0 \leq a \leq 3 \) and \( 0 \leq b \leq 3 \), we have: $$ F(a, b) = \int_0^a \int_0^b f(x, y) \, dy \, dx = c \left(\frac{a^3 b^2}{6} + \frac{a^3 b^3}{9}\right). $$ Since \( y = 3 \) is the maximum value for \( Y \), we have: $$ F_X(a) = F(a, 3) = c \left(\frac{9 a^3}{6} + 3 a^3\right) = \frac{9}{2} c a^3 = \frac{a^3}{27}. $$ Sachin Mittal 1 answered May 26, 2024 Sachin Mittal 1 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Toss a fair coin 3 times. Let $X$ be the number of heads on the first toss, $Y$ the total number of heads on the last two tosses, and $F$ the number of heads on the first two tosses. Which of the following is correct regarding the covariances $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(X, F)$ ? $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=\frac{1}{4}, \operatorname{Cov}(X, F)=0$ $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=0, \operatorname{Cov}(X, F)=\frac{1}{4}$ $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=0, \operatorname{Cov}(X, F)=\frac{1}{2}$ $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=0, \operatorname{Cov}(X, F)=\frac{1}{8}$
questions.questionHtml:
Toss a fair coin 3 times. Let $X$ be the number of heads on the first toss, $Y$ the total number of heads on the last two tosses, and $F$ the number of heads on the first two tosses.
Which of the following is correct regarding the covariances $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(X, F)$ ?

  1. $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=\frac{1}{4}, \operatorname{Cov}(X, F)=0$
     
  2. $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=0, \operatorname{Cov}(X, F)=\frac{1}{4}$
     
  3. $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=0, \operatorname{Cov}(X, F)=\frac{1}{2}$
     
  4. $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=0, \operatorname{Cov}(X, F)=\frac{1}{8}$
questions.explanation: X is 1st Toss Y is Last 2 Tosses F is First 2 Tosses. All 3 tosses are independent to each other. It can be seen that X and Y are independent to each other as they do not have any common tosses. So, Cov(X,Y) = 0 Cov(X,F) != 0 and Cov(F,Y) != 0 for the same reason as they have one common toss. X and F are dependent on each other because of 1st Toss. Therefore, Cov(X,F) = Cov(X,X) = Var(X) Since X is Bernoulli Distribution. Therefore, Cov(X,F) = Var(X) = p(1-p) = (0.5)(0.5) = 0.25 Similarly Cov(F,Y) = $0.25$ too as they are dependent because of $2$nd Toss only. Method 2: Cov(X,F) = Cov(X, X + 2nd Toss) = Cov(X,X) + Cov(X,2) Since Cov(X,2) = 0 as they are independent to each other. Therefore Cov(X,X) = Var(X) = $0.25$ GO Classes Support answered Jan 9, 2025 • edited Jul 15, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes Support comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 1 1 vote Toss a fair coin three times.   1. If $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=0$, then $X$ and $Y$ are independent.
     
  2. If $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=0$, then $X$ and $Y$ are not independent.
     
  3. If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=0$.
     
  4. If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) \neq 0$.

options.label: A
options.text: If $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=0$, then $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

options.label: B
options.text: If $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=0$, then $X$ and $Y$ are not independent.

options.label: C
options.text: If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=0$.

options.label: D
options.text: If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) \neq 0$.

questions.explanation: Aren't options A and C are same? sivasaiprasad answered Jun 3, 2024 sivasaiprasad comment Share Follow See 1 comment 1 1 comment reply suryakumarus commented Nov 14, 2024 reply Follow flag no 0 0 reply Share Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes If $A$ and $B$ are independent, then $E[XY] = E[X].E[Y]$ $Cov(A,B) = E[XY] - E[X].E[Y] = E[X].E[Y] - E[X].E[Y] = 0$ So, Option C is True. If $Cov(A,B) = 0,$ then we cannot comment anything on the independence. It may or may not be independent. For $A$ and $B$ to be independent. $P(A|B) = P(A)$ needs to be True. questions.questionText: Let $U$ be uniformly distributed over $(0,1)$ and let $V$ be uniformly distributed over $(0, U)$. Find $E[V \mid U=u]$. $E[V \mid U=u]=u$ $E[V \mid U=u]=\frac{u}{4}$ $E[V \mid U=u]=\frac{u}{2}$ $E[V \mid U=u]=\frac{u}{3}$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $U$ be uniformly distributed over $(0,1)$ and let $V$ be uniformly distributed over $(0, U)$.
Find $E[V \mid U=u]$.

  1. $E[V \mid U=u]=u$
     
  2. $E[V \mid U=u]=\frac{u}{4}$
     
  3. $E[V \mid U=u]=\frac{u}{2}$
     
  4. $E[V \mid U=u]=\frac{u}{3}$
questions.explanation: Given $U=u, V$ is uniformly distributed over $(0, u)$. The mean of a uniform random variable on the interval $(0, u)$ is: $E[V \mid U=u]=\frac{0+u}{2}=\frac{u}{2}$ Thus, the conditional expectation $E[V \mid U=u]$ is $\frac{u}{2}$. questions.questionText: ​​​​​​When six unbiased dice are rolled simultaneously, the probability of getting all distinct numbers $(i.e., 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, \text{and }   6)$ is $\dfrac{1}{324}$ $\dfrac{5}{324}$ $\dfrac{7}{324}$ $\dfrac{11}{324}$
questions.questionHtml:
​​​​​​When six unbiased dice are rolled simultaneously, the probability of getting all distinct numbers $(i.e., 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, \text{and }   6)$ is

  1. $\dfrac{1}{324}$

  2. $\dfrac{5}{324}$

  3. $\dfrac{7}{324}$

  4. $\dfrac{11}{324}$
questions.explanation: We have 6 unbiased dices that are rolled simultaneously. As, dices are unbiased. Then, P(x) = $1/6$ where x $\in$ {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. When a dice is rolled then any number out of 6 can show up. So, with 1 dice we have 6 possible outcomes. And, when we have 6 dices and each dices have 6 choices then total possible outcomes = $6^{6}$. Total cases : $6^{6}$. Now, we want different numbers on all 6 dices. So, combination like these are our feasible cases : (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), (1, 3, 5, 2, 4, 6), (2, 4, 6, 5, 3, 1) , (6, 1, 3, 5. 4, 2), - - - - - - - - - - , (6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1) How many such feasible case? It will be 6! = 720 Feasible cases : 6! = 720 So, Required Probability : Feasible cases / Total Cases = 6! / $6^{6}$. = 5 / 324. Hence , Option B is correct Answer.

Consider the following statements P, Q, R, and S: (P) : \( X \) is a standard normal random variable. (Q) : The conditional distribution of \( X \) given \( Y \) is normal. (R) : The conditional distribution of \( X + Y\) is normal. (S) : \( X - Y \) has mean 0. Which of the above statements ALWAYS hold TRUE? (A) both P and Q (B) both Q and R (C) both Q and S (D) both P and S
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose \( X \) and \( Y \) are two random variables such that \( aX + bY \) is a normal random variable for all \( a, b \) in \( \mathbf{R} \). Consider the following statements P, Q, R, and S:
(P) : \( X \) is a standard normal random variable.
(Q) : The conditional distribution of \( X \) given \( Y \) is normal.
(R) : The conditional distribution of \( X + Y\) is normal.
(S) : \( X - Y \) has mean 0.

Which of the above statements ALWAYS hold TRUE?
(A) both P and Q

(B) both Q and R

(C) both Q and S

(D) both P and S
questions.explanation: (B), both Q and R always hold true.   Statement P: \(X\) doesn't necessarily have to be a standard normal random variable (mean of 0 and variance of 1). It could have a different mean or variance and still satisfy the condition that \(aX + bY\) is normal for all \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\). Therefore, P is not always true. Statement Q: If \(aX + bY\) is normal for all \(a, b\), then in particular, \(Y = 0 \cdot X + 1 \cdot Y\) is normal. This implies that the conditional distribution of \(X\) given \(Y\) is also normal. Therefore, Q is always true. Statement R: Similar to Q, if \(aX + bY\) is normal for all \(a, b\), then \(X + Y = 1 \cdot X + 1 \cdot Y\) is normal. This implies that the conditional distribution of \(X + Y\) is normal. Therefore, R is always true. Statement S: There's no guarantee that \(X - Y\) has mean 0. It could have a non-zero mean and still satisfy the condition that \(aX + bY\) is normal for all \(a, b\). Therefore, S is not always true.   rajveer43 answe

questions.explanation: To find the mean of the minimum of independent exponential random variables, we can use the fact that the minimum of exponential random variables follows an exponential distribution with a rate equal to the sum of the rates of the individual exponentials. Let \(X_i\) denote the exponential random variable with mean \(1/i\) for \(i = 1, 2, 3, 4\). The rate parameter \(\lambda_i\) for each \(X_i\) is given by \(\lambda_i = 1/(1/i) = i\). The minimum \(Y = \min(X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4)\) has a rate parameter \(\lambda_Y\) equal to the sum of the individual rates: \[ \lambda_Y = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 + \lambda_4 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. \] Therefore, \(Y\) follows an exponential distribution with mean \(1/\lambda_Y\): \[ \text{Mean of } Y = \frac{1}{\lambda_Y} = \frac{1}{10}. \] So, the mean of \(Y\) is \(\frac{1}{10}\). rajveer43 answered Jan 11, 2024 rajveer43 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.explanation: Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE): Likelihood Function: The likelihood function is the joint probability density function of the observed data, viewed as a function of the parameter \( \theta \). In this case, the \(X_i\) are independent, so the likelihood function is the product of their individual density functions: \[ L(\theta) = \prod f_X(x_i; \theta) = \theta^n \exp(-\theta \sum (x_i - 1)) \] Log-Likelihood: Taking the logarithm of the likelihood function simplifies calculations: \[ \ln L(\theta) = n \ln(\theta) - \theta \sum (x_i - 1) \] Derivative: To find the MLE, we differentiate the log-likelihood with respect to \( \theta \) and set it equal to 0: \[ \frac{d}{d\theta} \ln L(\theta) = \frac{n}{\theta} - \sum (x_i - 1) = 0 \] Solve for \( \theta \): Solving for \( \theta \) gives: \[ \theta = \frac{n}{\sum (x_i - 1)} = \frac{n}{nX - n} = \frac{1}{X - 1} \]   rajveer43 answered Jan 11, 2024 rajveer43 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a

questions.explanation: Central Limit Theorem: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) states that the sum or average of a large number of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables, regardless of their underlying distribution, will tend to be normally distributed as the sample size increases. Applying CLT to Poisson Distribution: In this case, we have a sequence of i.i.d. Poisson(\(\lambda\)) variables. The mean of a Poisson(\(\lambda\)) distribution is \(\lambda\), and the variance is also \(\lambda\). We're considering the average of these variables, \(W_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum X_i\). As \(n\) approaches infinity, the CLT tells us that the distribution of \(W_n\) will approach a normal distribution with mean \(\lambda\) and variance \(\frac{\lambda}{n}\). questions.questionText: Let $X$ be a non constant positive random variable such that $E(X)=9$. Then which of the following statements is correct A) $E(1X+1)>0.1$    and  $P(X≥10)≤0.9$ B) $E(1X+1)<0.1$  and $P(X≥10)≤0.9$ C) $E(1X+1)>0.1$  and $P(X≥10)>0.9$ D) $E(1X+1)<0.1  and P(X≥10)>0.9$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $X$ be a non constant positive random variable such that $E(X)=9$. Then which of the following statements is correct

A) $E(1X+1)>0.1$
   and  $P(X≥10)≤0.9$

B) $E(1X+1)<0.1$
 and $P(X≥10)≤0.9$

C) $E(1X+1)>0.1$
 and $P(X≥10)>0.9$

D) $E(1X+1)<0.1
 and P(X≥10)>0.9$
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) $E(1/X+1) > 0.1$ and $P(X ≥ 10) ≤ 0.9$ . Here's the explanation: 1. $E(1/X+1) > 0.1$: Non-constant positive variable:  Since X is non-constant and always positive, 1/X will also be positive but never exceed 1 (because X is at least 1). Lower bound for expected value:  This means that E(1/X) will always be a positive number less than or equal to 1. Adding 1:  When we add 1 to E(1/X), we get a value greater than 1, which is definitely more than 0.1. Therefore, E(1/X+1) > 0.1 is always true. 2. $P(X ≥ 10) ≤ 0.9$: Expected value:  E(X) = 9 indicates that X is expected to be around 9 on average. Probability of exceeding 10:  Since X is non-constant, it can take values both below and above 9. However, the probability of it being significantly larger than 9 (like 10 or more) cannot be too high, as it would contradict the expected value. Calculate the probability that exactly two calls will be received during each of the first 5 minutes of the hour.   the given solution is: Assume that “N” is the number of calls received during 1 minute. questions.questionHtml:
Let $X$ be a set containing $n$ elements. Three subsets $A, B, C$ of $X$ are chosen at random. The probability that $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}$ and C are pairwise disjoint, is

A $\frac{{ }^{2 n} C_{n}}{2^{n}}$
(B) $\frac{1}{2^{n}}$
Correct Option

Solution :
(b)

For each element $a_{i} \in_{X^{\prime}}$
\[
\left.\begin{array}{l}
\text { either } a_{i} \notin A \text { and } a_{i} \notin B \text { and } a_{i} \notin C \\
\text { or, } a_{i} \notin A \text { and } a_{i} \notin B \text { and } a_{i} \notin C \\
\text { or, } a_{i} \notin A \text { and } a_{i} \notin B \text { and } a_{i} \notin C \\
\text { or, } \quad a_{i} \notin A \text { and } a_{i} \notin B \text { and } a_{i} \notin C
\end{array}\right\} 4 \text { choices for } a_{i}
\]

Therefore required probability $=\frac{4^{n}}{8^{n}}=\frac{1}{2^{n}}$
$\therefore$ Option (b) is correct.

In a multiuser operating system, $20$ requests are made to use a particular resource per hour, on an average. The probability that no request is made in $45$ minutes is

  1. $\mathrm{e}^{-15}$
  2. $\mathrm{e}^{-5}$
  3. $1-\mathrm{e}^{-5}$
  4. $1-\mathrm{e}^{-10}$
questions.explanation: source for this – GO CLASSES Rajatagrawal answered Jul 31, 2023 Rajatagrawal comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes We need to find the probability of no events (i.e., x = 0) in 45 minutes, which is 3/4th of an hour.  The average rate of events per hour is given as 20. - So, λ = 20 events per hour. We need to find the probability of 0 events in 3/4th of an hour. - So, the time interval is 3/4th of an hour, and the average rate of events per interval is λ = 20 * 3/4 = 15. Substituting these values in the Poisson distribution formula, we get: P(0) = (e^-15 * 15^0) / 0! = e^-15 Therefore, the probability that no requests are made in 45 minutes is e^-15, which is approximately 3.06 * 10^-7.  Answer: - The correct answer is option 'A' (e^-15).

questions.questionHtml:
Suppose that $X, Y$, and $Z$ are independent random variables. $\mathbf{E}[X]=1, \mathbf{E}[Y]=2$, and $\mathbf{E}[Z]=3$. $\operatorname{var}(X)=1$, $\operatorname{var}(Y)=2,$ and $\operatorname{var}(Z)=3$. Compute the value of the following expression:
$$
\mathbf{E}[2 X+3 Y-Z-10]+\operatorname{var}(Y-2 X+2 Z)
$$

  1. $5$
     
  2. $13$
     
  3. $-3$
     
  4. $10$
questions.explanation: This question is based on the expectation and variance properties. We know,                 E[constant] = constant                 E[constant * X] = constant * E[X]        $E[2X + 3Y - Z - 10]$ $= 2E[X] + 3E[X] - E[Z] - 10$ $= 2*1 + 3*2 - 3 - 10$ $= 2 + 6 - 3 - 10 = -5$   Now, we know,               Var[constant] = 0                Var[constant * X] = X^2 Var[X]      (Note : if there is a -ve sign with the constant, take the sign outside too)   Var[Y – 2X + 2Z] = Var[Y] + (-2^-2)Var[X] + (2^2)Var[Z] = 2 + 4*1 + 4*3 = 18   Therefore, -5 + 18 = 13. chokostar answered Apr 29, 2023 chokostar comment Share Follow See all 3 Comments 3 3 Comments reply Sachin Mittal 1 commented Apr 29, 2023 reply Follow flag Nice answer 2 2 reply Share myDarkPassenger commented Apr 30, 2023 reply

questions.questionHtml:
Let $X$ be a discrete uniform random variable. It has a probability mass function (PMF) $P(X=k)=\dfrac{1}{n}$ for $k=1, \ldots, n,$ the expected value $\mathbb{E}[X]$ is given by

questions.explanation: Expectation E is given by, $\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{n} k. P(X=k)$ Now, as per the question,           $P(X = k ) = 1/n$  $where$  $k = 1,\ldots n$ Therefore,  $E(X) = 1/n * (1+2+3+\ldots n)$ $E(X) = 1/n * n(n+1)/2$ $E(X) = (n+1)/2$   Option C is the correct answer.

questions.questionHtml:
Let $X$ be Bernoulli random variables with parameter $p (\text{i.e}., P(X=1)=p, P(X=0)=1-p)$.

Define a random variable $Y=2^X 3^{1-X}$.

What is $E[Y]?$

  1. $p$
  2. $2^p$
  3. $3-p$
  4. $\log _6 p$
questions.explanation: When $X=1, Y=2$ and when $X=0, Y=3$. So $Y$ takes two values. $$ P(Y=k)= \begin{cases}p & \text { When } k=2 \\ 1-p & \text { When } k=3\end{cases} $$ $$ E[Y]=2 \mathrm{p}+3(1-\mathrm{p})=3-p. $$ GO Classes answered Apr 28, 2023 • edited Apr 28, 2023 by Lakshman Bhaiya GO Classes comment Share Follow See all 2 Comments 2 2 Comments reply pavansan commented Dec 19, 2024 reply Follow flag anyone can pls explain bit more clearly not getting 0 0 reply Share Hazard commented Jul 4, 2025 reply Follow flag First make a Probability Distribution function , Where x=0 then y=3 and prob. is 1-p. x=1 then y=2 and prob. is p. questions.questionHtml:
Let $X$ be a random variable with $\mathrm{PDF}$
$$f(x)= \begin{cases}C\left(1-x^2\right) & -1 <x<1\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
What is $C ?$

  1. $1 / 2$
  2. $1 / 3$
  3. $1 / 4$
  4. $3 / 4$
questions.explanation: By normalization $\displaystyle{}\int_{-1}^1 C\left(1-x^2\right) d x=\left.C\left(x-x^3 / 3\right)\right|_{-1} ^1=1$ So $C(2-2 / 3)=4 C / 3=1$. So $C=3 / 4$. questions.questionText: Let $X_i$ are independent discrete uniform random variables defined for consecutive integers in the interval $[1, n]$. That is $P(X_i=j)=1 / n$ for any $i$ and $j$ in $[1, n]$. Let $Y=\min \{X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\}$. Find $P(Y>k)$ for some $k = n-1$. $(1 / n)^ \mathrm{n}$ $(1-1 / n)^ n$ $1-(1 / n)^ n$ None of these
questions.questionHtml:
Let $X_i$ are independent discrete uniform random variables defined for consecutive integers in the interval $[1, n]$. That is $P(X_i=j)=1 / n$ for any $i$ and $j$ in $[1, n]$.

Let $Y=\min \{X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\}$.

Find $P(Y>k)$ for some $k = n-1$.

  1. $(1 / n)^ \mathrm{n}$
  2. $(1-1 / n)^ n$
  3. $1-(1 / n)^ n$
  4. None of these
questions.explanation: Given, $k=n-1$ $P(Y>k)=P(Y>n-1)$. Since, Y is a random variable that takes values from $[1, n]$, $P(Y>n-1)=P(Y=n)$. $Y$ equals $n$ when each random variable $X_{i}$ equals to n. Since each $X_{i}$ is independent, $P(Y=n)$ = $\prod P(X_{i}=n)$ for $i$ in $[1, n]$. $P(Y=n)$ = $\frac{1}{n}$ x $\frac{1}{n}$ x …...$n$ times. $P(Y=n)$ = $(\frac{1}{n})^{n}$ Suraj Reddy answered Apr 28, 2023 Suraj Reddy comment Share Follow See 1 comment 1 1 comment reply chokostar commented Apr 29, 2023 reply Follow flag The best part of this question was : P(Y > n – 1) = P(Y = n) I wish this came to my mind during the test too :(

questions.questionText: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables, such that $X$ has probability mass function $P(X=x)=(1 / 3)(2 / 3)^{x-1}$ for integers $x \geq 1,$  and $Y$ has probability mass function $P(Y=y)=(2 / 5)(3 / 5)^{y-1}$ for integers $y \geq 1$. Find $P(X=Y)$. $1 / 9$ $2 / 9$ $1 / 3$ $1 / 2$
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables,

such that $X$ has probability mass function $P(X=x)=(1 / 3)(2 / 3)^{x-1}$ for integers $x \geq 1,$ 

and $Y$ has probability mass function $P(Y=y)=(2 / 5)(3 / 5)^{y-1}$ for integers $y \geq 1$.

Find $P(X=Y)$.

  1. $1 / 9$
  2. $2 / 9$
  3. $1 / 3$
  4. $1 / 2$
questions.explanation: We compute $P(X=Y)$ $$ \begin{aligned} & =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} P(X=Y=n) \\ & =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} P(X=n) P(Y=n) \\ & =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(1 / 3)(2 / 3)^{n-1}(2 / 5)(3 / 5)^{n-1} \\ & =\frac{(1 / 3)(2 / 5)}{1-(2 / 3)(3 / 5)}=2 / 9 . \end{aligned} $$ GO Classes answered Apr 28, 2023 GO Classes comment Share Follow See 1 comment 1 1 comment reply Balasarath BS commented May 13, 2024 reply Follow flag For folks who are wondering how we ended up with the last line, we used  infinite series GP formula . 9 9 reply Share Please log in or register to add a comment. 10 10 votes Suppose that \( X \) and \( Y \) are independent random variables, such that \( X \) has probability mass function \( P(X = x) = \left( \frac{1}{3} \right) \left( \frac{2}{3} \right)^{x-1} \) for integers \( x \geq 1 \), and \( Y \) has probability mass function \( P(Y = y) = \left( \frac{2}{5} \right) \left( \frac{3}{5} \right)^{y-1} \) for integers \( y \geq 1 \).
